name: Fatima Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on a fit-out crew, which means we do the electrics when a shop or an office gets gutted and rebuilt. Right now it's a phone shop in the shopping centre, so we work nights, ten till six, when the mall is shut. I'm up a ladder in the ceiling most of the shift, fixing cable tray, which is the metal trough the cables run along, and pulling cable for the lights. The foreman, Stelian, hands out the drawings and I do what he tells me.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's the same routine on every job. You know where you are with cable tray. What wears me out is the nights, and the gaps between jobs. The firm only keeps us on while there's a contract, and last January I had three weeks with no work and no pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So nothing changes. Okay. That's what I'd guess would happen anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, a bit. People at the mall canteen were going on about AI taking over and I never saw it. I'd say let's get back to work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My real worry stays the same: the gaps. Nobody needs AI to take my job when the fit-out contracts dry up every January on their own. I live alone, so if work stops, it's all on me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep saving for the January gap, about 100 a week in the busy months. I'd keep my head down and turn up every shift so Stelian picks me for the next contract. I wouldn't change anything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Same as always, really. It's not new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How many months could you cover if work stopped?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About three, maybe a bit more if I stopped eating out. Rent is the big one, my flat's 40 percent of my pay. After that I'd move back to my parents', which I really don't want at 27.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the job feel more secure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A permanent contract, even on less money. I'd take steady over more any day. But the firm won't do that for juniors.

say: I'd say I **never believed** the AI hype from the mall canteen.
I'd tell the crew it's time to **get back to work**.
think: I think the **January gaps** threaten me more than AI does.
I think living **alone** puts every lost week on me.
do: Save about **100 a week** in busy months for the gaps.
Turn up **every shift** so Stelian picks me next.
feel: I feel **uneasy**, the same as always.
S0.quote: Nobody needs AI to take my job when the fit-out contracts dry up every January on their own.
fieldNote: Fatima's pressure is **project-based work** with unpaid gaps, not AI.
Her rent is about **40 percent** of her pay, with only three months saved.
She'd trade pay for a **permanent contract**.

steps.text: Save about 100 a week during busy months for the January gap
Turn up for every night shift so Stelian picks her for the next contract

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Writing and booking and that. That's office stuff. I don't touch any of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's sad for the office people but it won't touch us much. I'd say the trades are still the trades. I wouldn't post anything, I don't post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it might touch us sideways. If AI cuts office jobs, fewer companies need fancy new offices, and that's half our fit-out work gone. That's what bothers me, not a robot on my ladder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save harder, maybe 120 a week. I'd ask Stelian if the firm's doing more shop or more office work, so I know where it's heading. I'd look at the maintenance firms near me, just to know they're there, but I wouldn't apply yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit more than before. Like hearing the boss is having meetings behind a closed door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd look at maintenance firms but not apply. Why not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because changing jobs is a risk, and I don't like risk. I'd be the new one again, and the new one gets let go first. I'd only move if Stelian told me the office jobs had dried up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try any of the AI tools yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I don't use them now and I don't see why I would. My job is in the ceiling, not on a screen.

say: I'd say the trades **won't be touched** much by any of it.
I'd say it's **sad** for the office workers who lose out.
think: I think fewer office jobs mean fewer **office fit-outs** for us.
I fear losing **half our work** that way.
do: Ask Stelian whether work is shifting to **shops or offices**.
Watch **maintenance firms** nearby but not apply yet.
feel: I feel **more uneasy**, like the boss meeting behind closed doors.
S1.quote: If AI cuts office jobs, fewer companies need fancy new offices, and that's half our fit-out work gone.
fieldNote: Fatima sees an **indirect hit**: fewer offices to fit out.
Her dislike of risk keeps her from **changing employer** early.

steps.text: Ask Stelian whether shop or office contracts are growing
Keep working nights on the fit-out crew

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots by 2031. That's four years after I'd have finished my licence. If I've finished it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say nobody knows how this plays out, so don't panic. That's what I'd say, anyway. Inside I'd be panicking a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think fit-out is exactly what robots would do first. A robot that bolts cable tray to a shop ceiling all night, without a break, is worth more to my firm than me. Same ceiling heights, same tray, every job. I'd be one of the first gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut everything: no eating out, cancel the gym, maybe give up the flat and move back to my parents' to save rent. I'd try to get onto the maintenance side, the repair calls, because every building's different. And I'd finish the licence however hard it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying awake, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd move back to your parents'. What would that be like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum would be happy and I'd be miserable. My old room still has the pink wallpaper. But it would save me nearly all my rent, and that's two more years of cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said you wouldn't use AI tools. In this one, would you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, if Stelian said I had to. But I'd be bad at it, and I'd know I was bad at it. I'd rather spend the time learning repairs by hand.

say: I'd tell people at work **not to panic** yet.
I'd say **nobody knows** how it really plays out.
I'd keep my **real fear** to myself.
think: I think **fit-out** is what robots do first, because every ceiling is the same.
I'd be among the **first gone** from my firm.
do: Cut **eating out and gym**, and maybe give up the flat.
Move to the **maintenance side** where every building differs.
Finish the **licence** however hard it is.
feel: I feel **alarmed**, and I'd be lying awake.
S2.quote: A robot that bolts cable tray to a shop ceiling all night, without a break, is worth more to my firm than me.
fieldNote: Fatima's **say and think** split sharply here: calm in public, panicking privately.
She judges **repetitive fit-out** as robot-ready work.
Moving back to her **parents** is her real safety net.

steps.text: Cancel the gym and stop eating out
Give up the flat and move back to her parents' home
Apply to a maintenance firm doing repair call-outs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, robots in 2034. Okay. Still fast, but I'd have more time to get out of fit-out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, again, don't panic. Get your licence and you'll be okay. That's what Stelian would say too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd still be in trouble, just later. Five years gives me just long enough to get good at the one thing the robots will do first. Unless I move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my licence in the next year, then look for a job in maintenance in year two or three. I'd save, 120 a week, not panic-cut. I'd keep the flat, for now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Less than the fast one, but I'd still think about it every January.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you take the step to maintenance, instead of waiting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A firm offering a permanent contract. If one did, I'd go. If not, I'd wait for Stelian to tell me the robots were coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone you'd talk this over with?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad. He was a bus mechanic for 30 years and saw the buses go electric. He'd tell me to move early and stop being stubborn, and he'd be right, and I'd still drag my feet.

say: I'd tell people again **not to panic**.
I'd say get your **licence** and you'll be okay, like Stelian says.
think: I think I'm still in **trouble, just later**.
I'd only just get good at what **robots do first**.
do: Finish my **licence** in the next year.
Look for **maintenance work** in year two or three.
Keep saving **120 a week** and keep the flat.
feel: I feel **anxious**, and I'd think about it every January.
S3.quote: Five years gives me just long enough to get good at the one thing the robots will do first.
fieldNote: Fatima would move only for a **permanent contract**.
Her father, a **bus mechanic**, would push her to move early.
She admits she'd **drag her feet** anyway.

steps.text: Finish the licence within a year
Apply to maintenance firms offering permanent contracts by year three

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, robots in 2039. I'd be 40. That's long enough to be properly settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and lots can happen. I'd say it's not worth worrying about yet. I'd mean it, mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd be fine until my late thirties, but then fit-out would go, and maybe me with it. I'd love to tell you I'll plan ahead for ten years, but honestly I'd wait until year eight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my licence and keep working with Stelian's crew. I'd try for a permanent contract. I'd save a bit, the same 100 a week. I don't think I'd do much else at first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little anxious still, but quieter. Like a bill I know is coming next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait until year eight. What would year eight look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably me seeing the first robot on a site and finally ringing round the maintenance firms. Too late, maybe. But that's how I am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would get you to move sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If someone gave me a sure thing. A job with a contract and a pension. I'm not the type to jump without something to land on.

say: I'd say ten years is a **long time** and lots can happen.
I'd say it's **not worth worrying** about yet.
think: I think fit-out work goes in my **late thirties**, maybe with me.
I'd honestly **wait until year eight** to act.
do: Finish my **licence** and stay with Stelian's crew.
feel: I feel **quietly anxious**, like a bill coming next year.
S4.quote: I'd love to tell you I'll plan ahead for ten years, but honestly I'd wait until year eight.
fieldNote: Fatima knows she'd **wait too long**, and says so.
She needs a **sure thing** before she'll move.
Even with a decade, the **gaps** and fit-out exposure keep her anxious.

steps.text: Finish the licence and stay on Stelian's fit-out crew
Ask the firm for a permanent contract

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because fit-out is the first thing robots would take, and I'd only just have my licence. What would help is a permanent contract somewhere, and some help to move into maintenance before it's too late, a paid course or a firm that takes on juniors.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the gaps. People talk about robots, but nobody asks what an electrician does in January when the mall has no contracts.

headlineQuote: People talk about robots, but nobody asks what an electrician does in January when the mall has no contracts.
portrait: Fatima is a **27-year-old junior** on a night-shift shop and office fit-out crew.
She lives **alone**, with about three months saved and unpaid gaps every January.
She **avoids risk** and AI tools, and wants a permanent contract above all.
She grows **alarmed** when robots could reach repetitive fit-out fast, and admits she'd act late.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, since fit-out goes first and she'd only just be licensed.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid course** or firm to move juniors into maintenance.
